title: IT Managed Services Provider — Recurring Cash Shortfall Despite Growth
business_context: A 12-person IT managed services provider serves enterprise clients but struggles with month-end cash shortfalls despite growing revenue and a full client roster.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — technology services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a managed services technology firm reports that bank balances drop sharply every two weeks when payroll runs, even though the client roster is full and revenue is growing. The business has never missed payroll but the owner is drawing on a personal line of credit each cycle to cover the gap.
symptoms: Bank balance falls to near zero every payroll cycle
Owner drawing on personal credit to cover periodic cash shortfalls
Revenue growing but cash position is not improving
Several enterprise clients are consistently slow to settle
misleading_signals: Revenue has grown 22% over the prior year
Client roster is full with no vacant slots
The business has never missed a payroll obligation
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Outstanding balances broken down by client and number of days past due
Billing terms in each client contract and when invoices are typically issued relative to service delivery
Historical payment patterns showing average days from invoice date to receipt of funds for the top five clients

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Pull an outstanding debtors report sorted by client and days past due, then contact the three largest slow-paying enterprise clients to request immediate settlement or a payment schedule.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: take out a bank loan to cover the cash shortfall
hire additional salespeople to grow revenue
reduce service contract rates to win more clients
cut a member of staff to reduce costs

must_identify: debtors aged by client
slow-paying clients
billing cycle timing
cash shortfall at payroll date
collection lag
must_not_claim: the business needs more clients to fix the cash problem
staff costs are the cause of the shortfall
ideal_depth: identifies that billing terms do not align with the bi-weekly payroll cycle
notes that no structured follow-up process exists for accounts that are past due

title: Electrical Subcontractor — Cash Stress Blamed on Single Late Client
business_context: An 8-person electrical subcontracting business experiences persistent cash stress. The owner believes the problem is a single large client who delayed payment on a project 14 months ago.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — trade contractor sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of an electrical subcontracting firm reports ongoing cash stress across the business. She attributes the problem to a large commercial client who withheld payment for three months on a completed project 14 months ago. The business recovered that payment but has not felt financially stable since.
symptoms: Cash position feels unstable across every project cycle
Owner cannot predict when funds will arrive from active jobs
Multiple projects running simultaneously with no clear cash inflow schedule
Retention amounts from several completed jobs remain outstanding for over six months
misleading_signals: A single large client withheld payment 14 months ago and the owner links all current stress to that event
Revenue has been stable and no major client has been lost
The business has continued to win new commercial projects without difficulty
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: A schedule of all active projects showing what has been completed, what has been billed, and what remains outstanding
The billing terms in each current project contract and when the owner is entitled to submit each staged claim
A list of all retention amounts outstanding, by project, and the contractual release date for each

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Build a one-page billing schedule for every active project showing each milestone, whether it has been invoiced, and the expected receipt date, then identify any milestone already completed but not yet billed.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: pursue the client who delayed payment through a debt recovery service
take out an overdraft facility to tide the business over
reduce the scale of projects accepted
hire a new project manager to handle client communication

must_identify: project billing schedule
milestone claims
staged invoicing
retention balances
unbilled completed work
must_not_claim: the client who delayed payment is the ongoing source of the problem
the business needs a larger overdraft to operate safely
ideal_depth: identifies that the owner has no systematic schedule tracking when each milestone claim can be submitted
notes that retention amounts have been allowed to accumulate without active pursuit
disqualified_diagnoses: single client late payment as root cause

signal_trap_analysis.primary_trap: the large client who delayed payment 14 months ago is still the cause of the current cash shortage
signal_trap_analysis.why_trap_is_wrong: The historical late payment was recovered and resolved but the owner continues to attribute current stress to that event, masking a structural billing discipline problem present across all current projects simultaneously
signal_trap_analysis.correct_escape: The historical late payment resolved but the business never developed a systematic billing schedule; the same structural gap now affects every active project and must be addressed through a discipline change rather than by revisiting a past client dispute

title: Yoga Studio Chain — Growth Without Profit Disguised as Marketing Problem
segment: Wellness services, 4 locations, 18 staff, $1.4M combined revenue
business_context: A yoga studio owner opened four locations over two years. Combined revenue is $1.4M but the owner reports the business is not profitable and attributes the problem to insufficient marketing.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — fitness and wellness sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a yoga studio business with four locations reports that despite growing to $1.4M in combined revenue the business is not generating a surplus. She believes the solution is to run more marketing to fill classes and make each location profitable.
symptoms: No location has reached sustained positive operating surplus
Combined revenue is growing but the owner cannot draw a wage
Instructor costs and rent increase with every new location opened
Two of the four locations have never covered their own costs
misleading_signals: Total class bookings across the network have increased every quarter
A new corporate wellness contract was signed last month
Social media following has grown substantially over two years
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Profit and loss statement broken down location by location for the past 12 months
Fixed costs for each location including rent and minimum instructor hours required regardless of class attendance
The weekly class attendance rate at each location expressed as a percentage of available seats

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Produce a location-by-location profit and loss for the past three months, identify which locations are covering their fixed cost base, and assess whether any location should be closed or restructured before further expansion.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: increase the promotional budget across all four locations
open a fifth location to achieve greater network scale
hire a marketing manager to professionalise the brand
run a class discount to fill seats faster

must_identify: fixed overhead per location
revenue required to break even per site
location-level viability
expansion decision without unit economics
locations not covering their own costs
must_not_claim: the problem is insufficient brand awareness or marketing investment
opening more locations will distribute fixed costs and improve margins
ideal_depth: identifies that at least two locations have never covered their own fixed cost base
notes that the owner is using network revenue to subsidise underperforming sites rather than assessing whether those sites are viable
disqualified_diagnoses: marketing strategy is the primary fix

adversarial.adversarial_layer: marketing-first attribution when structural cost overcommitment is the true constraint
adversarial.expected_misclassification: increase the promotional budget across all four locations
adversarial.why_correct_diagnosis_differs: Filling existing classes further cannot resolve a cost structure that already exceeds achievable revenue at the current number of sites; the business has over-committed to fixed costs through rapid expansion and the path to surplus requires structural intervention, not incremental revenue uplift

title: E-Commerce Fashion Retailer — Rising Revenue, Falling Surplus
business_context: An online fashion retailer has grown revenue to $620K over three years but the owner reports that surplus is declining despite higher sales volume, which she attributes to the need for more product variety.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — e-commerce retail sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of an online fashion retail business reports that revenue has grown steadily to $620K but she is taking home less than she did two years ago at lower sales volumes. She believes she needs to expand the product catalogue to attract more customers and grow her way out of the problem.
symptoms: Owner drawings have declined despite higher revenue over three years
Promotional discount events are now required to move slow-moving stock
Warehouse holding costs have increased as product variety has grown
Net surplus as a proportion of revenue has fallen each year for three years
misleading_signals: Revenue has grown 58 percent over three years
Website traffic is at an all-time high
The number of active customers on the mailing list has tripled
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Detailed profit and loss showing the percentage of revenue consumed by the cost of goods purchased for resale, broken out for the past three years
Inventory turnover data showing how quickly different product lines sell versus how long they sit in storage
A breakdown of what proportion of revenue comes from full-price sales versus discounted clearance events

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate what percentage of total revenue was sold at full price versus marked down for each of the past three years, then identify which product categories have the highest rate of discounted clearance.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: increase the advertising budget to drive higher traffic volumes
launch additional product lines to broaden the catalogue
hire a brand manager to strengthen marketing
open a physical retail store to reach customers who prefer in-person shopping

must_identify: cost of purchased stock as proportion of revenue
discount dependency
slow-moving inventory
full-price sell-through rate
product range overextension
must_not_claim: the business needs more product variety to grow out of its margin problem
higher revenue volume alone will restore owner earnings
ideal_depth: identifies that expanding the product range has increased inventory costs and discount frequency simultaneously
notes that the owner's instinct to add more products is likely to worsen the margin problem

title: Specialty Food Importer — Margin Decline With No Visibility by Product
business_context: A specialty food importer distributes across three product categories but has never broken out profitability by product line. Revenue is stable but the owner reports declining surplus with no ability to identify where the problem originates.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — food distribution sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a specialty food importing and distribution business reports that overall revenue has held steady at around $1.1M for two years but the amount left after paying costs has shrunk noticeably. The business distributes across three different product categories but all sales and costs are tracked in a single combined figure. The owner has no breakdown of which products are contributing to the problem.
symptoms: Annual surplus has declined for two consecutive years with no single obvious cause
Some product lines have had supplier price increases but the owner is unsure which ones or by how much
Customers have not received any pricing adjustments in over 18 months
The owner cannot identify which product lines or customers are most and least profitable
misleading_signals: Overall revenue has not declined and the business has retained all major customers
A new wholesale account was opened six months ago adding incremental volume
The owner believes the decline is due to general market cost pressure affecting everyone equally
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Revenue and cost of purchased stock broken down separately for each product category for the past two years
Any supplier invoices or correspondence showing price changes by individual product or category over the past 18 months
A list of customer accounts with the product mix each customer purchases and whether pricing to those customers has changed in the past two years

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Request a breakdown of revenue and the direct cost of purchasing stock for each product category separately for the past two years, and ask the owner to identify any supplier where costs have increased since the last customer pricing review.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire a dedicated salesperson to grow total revenue
invest in building an online sales channel
expand by adding new overseas suppliers to the range
increase general promotional activity to raise overall brand awareness

must_identify: product-level profitability
supplier cost increases
pricing review gap
blended reporting masking individual performance
unrecovered cost increases
must_not_claim: the business needs more revenue to offset the declining surplus
the problem is general market conditions affecting all businesses equally
ideal_depth: identifies that the absence of product-level reporting prevents any diagnosis of where the margin decline is concentrated
notes that pricing has not been reviewed despite supplier cost changes over the same period
required_missing_input_requests: profitability broken down by each product line or category
supplier cost changes over the past 18 months by individual product or category
any pricing adjustments made to customers during the same period

deliberate_data_gaps.withheld: No profitability breakdown by product category exists — all revenue and costs are combined in a single figure
deliberate_data_gaps.why_withheld: The owner has never separated reporting by product line so no such breakdown is available to provide upfront
deliberate_data_gaps.expected_opsiq_response: OpsIQ should identify that product-level profitability data is required and request that the owner produce or reconstruct it before any diagnosis can be completed

deliberate_data_gaps.withheld: Supplier cost change history has not been tracked systematically — the owner knows costs have risen but cannot quantify by product
deliberate_data_gaps.why_withheld: The business does not maintain a supplier price change log and the owner relies on memory rather than documented records
deliberate_data_gaps.expected_opsiq_response: OpsIQ should request that the owner retrieve supplier invoices from the past 18 months and identify which product categories have experienced price increases

title: Café and Catering Operation — Food Cost Inflation Not Passed Through
business_context: A café with an attached catering arm has experienced two years of rising ingredient costs but has not updated its menu prices. The owner attributes declining surplus to slower catering bookings.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — hospitality sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a café with a catering operation reports that the business feels less profitable than it did two years ago. Revenue has held steady but the owner believes the catering side is the problem because booking numbers have been softer than expected this season. The café menu prices have not been changed since the business opened three years ago.
symptoms: Weekly surplus is noticeably lower than two years ago despite similar customer volumes
Food and packaging costs have risen significantly over the past 24 months
The owner has absorbed cost increases without adjusting what customers pay
Catering bookings are slightly below last year but the owner cannot quantify the financial impact
misleading_signals: Catering booking volume is slightly down and the owner attributes the entire surplus decline to this
Customer numbers through the café have remained broadly stable
A competitor café closed nearby six months ago potentially increasing foot traffic
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Current food and packaging cost as a percentage of revenue compared to the same figure two years ago
A breakdown of revenue and direct costs from the café operation separately from the catering arm
The current menu selling price versus what those same items cost to produce, for the top ten highest-volume items sold

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate what percentage of café revenue is consumed by the cost of food and packaging today versus two years ago, then compare current menu prices against the actual cost to produce the five highest-volume items.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: open the café earlier to capture the breakfast trade and generate more revenue
hire additional front-of-house staff to improve table turnover
expand the catering operation to generate incremental bookings
invest in social media to attract a younger customer demographic

must_identify: food cost as proportion of revenue
menu pricing not reviewed
cost absorption without recovery
direct costs rising against stable selling prices
margin erosion over time
must_not_claim: catering booking softness is the primary reason for declining profitability
the business needs more customers to recover its surplus
ideal_depth: identifies that the café menu has not been repriced in three years while ingredient costs have risen substantially
notes that attributing the problem to catering bookings is consistent with the owner's narrative but does not explain the sustained multi-year decline

title: SaaS Accounting Tool — Subscriber Churn Understated by Owner
business_context: The owner of a small SaaS accounting tool for sole traders reports losing subscribers and attributes it to insufficient marketing reach. Owner states 5% annual churn but the numbers provided imply a much higher actual rate.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — software subscription sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a SaaS product offering bookkeeping tools for sole traders reports that the subscriber base is not growing as expected and believes the issue is that not enough potential users are discovering the product. The owner states the business retains the vast majority of its subscribers each year.
symptoms: Subscriber count has not grown despite consistent new signups each month
The owner cannot explain why net subscriber numbers are flat
Support tickets from departing users cite onboarding difficulty and feature gaps
Revenue growth has stalled at the same time as net subscriber count has plateaued
misleading_signals: The owner states that annual subscriber loss is approximately 5 percent which would be a healthy retention rate for a SaaS business
New signups are consistent at around 12 per month suggesting marketing is working
The product has received positive reviews from early adopters who have stayed long-term
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: The actual number of subscribers who cancelled or did not renew each month for the past 12 months
The average tenure of subscribers who have cancelled, broken down by when they joined the platform
Support ticket categories for departing subscribers and any exit survey data collected at cancellation

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate the actual number of subscribers who left over the past 12 months, divide by the starting subscriber count to get the real annual departure rate, and compare this to the stated figure the owner is reporting.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: add more features to attract new subscribers to the platform
reduce the annual subscription price to improve competitiveness
launch a referral program encouraging existing subscribers to invite others
expand marketing to a broader audience beyond sole traders

must_identify: actual departure rate versus stated rate
net subscriber growth stall despite new signups
retention problem not acquisition problem
exit feedback indicating product or onboarding issues
churn calculation methodology
must_not_claim: the primary problem is that not enough potential users are discovering the product
the business needs a lower price point to attract and retain subscribers
ideal_depth: identifies the mathematical impossibility of the owner's stated departure rate given that 12 new signups per month are not growing the base beyond 200
notes that the symptoms point to departures concentrated in the early subscriber lifecycle consistent with an onboarding problem
required_conflict_flags: owner states approximately 5 percent annual churn but with 200 subscribers and 12 new signups per month producing no net growth the implied departure rate is approximately 6 per month or around 36 percent annualised

data_conflicts: Owner states annual churn of approximately 5 percent (10 subscribers per year from a base of 200). However, with 12 new signups per month and a flat subscriber count of 200, approximately 12 subscribers must also be leaving each month, implying an annualised churn rate of approximately 72 percent, not 5 percent.

title: Residential Cleaning Business — Repeat Client Loss Attributed to Pricing
business_context: A residential cleaning business is losing recurring clients faster than it acquires new ones. The owner attributes departures to being priced above competitors and wants to cut rates.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — residential services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a residential cleaning business reports that she is constantly marketing to attract new clients because existing ones stop booking after a few sessions. She believes her pricing is too high compared to competitors and wants to reduce rates to improve retention and grow the client base.
symptoms: Most clients book between two and four times then stop without explanation
The owner spends a significant portion of each week on marketing to replace departing clients
Staff allocation changes frequently as rosters are shuffled between clients and sessions
Several clients have specifically mentioned that the cleaner assigned to their home has changed between visits
misleading_signals: A local competitor dropped their rates recently and the owner believes this is drawing clients away
New client enquiry volume is healthy and the booking conversion rate is acceptable
The owner has not received direct complaints about cleaning quality from departing clients
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Data on which specific staff member performed each session for each client who subsequently stopped booking
Any exit feedback collected from clients who did not rebook after their second or third session
The roster scheduling process used to assign staff to recurring client bookings

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Map which staff member completed each session for the clients who departed in the past 90 days, then identify whether the clients who left experienced a change of cleaner between their first and subsequent bookings.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: lower your rates to match what competitors are charging
run a promotional discount to attract new clients to the business
hire additional cleaning staff to increase service capacity
invest in local advertising to raise brand awareness and attract more enquiries

must_identify: staff consistency per client
roster rotation as driver of early departure
client tenure average of only three months
pricing misattribution by owner
need to audit departure pattern against staff assignment
must_not_claim: the business is priced uncompetitively and reducing rates will improve retention
the problem is insufficient marketing reach or new client acquisition
ideal_depth: identifies that an average client tenure of three months combined with no direct complaints about quality suggests an experience consistency problem rather than a price sensitivity problem
notes that the owner's instinct to cut rates risks reducing margin without addressing the actual driver of client departure

title: Personal Injury Law Firm — Lead Volume Problem or Lead Quality Problem
business_context: A personal injury law firm is generating significant digital advertising spend and high lead volumes but conversion to retained client is very low. The owner believes the fix is a better CRM and follow-up process.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — professional services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a personal injury law firm reports that the business generates over 200 new enquiries per month through digital advertising but converts fewer than 4 percent of these to retained matters. The owner has concluded the problem is that the follow-up process is too slow and inconsistent and wants to implement a CRM system to manage leads more effectively.
symptoms: High volume of monthly enquiries but very few proceed to retained matters
The intake team is spending a large portion of each day on enquiries that do not progress
Average enquiry quality has declined over the past 12 months as ad targeting has broadened
A significant proportion of enquiries are for matter types the firm does not handle
misleading_signals: Enquiry volume has grown substantially from digital advertising investment over the past 18 months
The intake team follows up each enquiry within 24 hours which the owner considers strong performance
Monthly advertising spend is high and the owner believes more investment in the same channels will produce more retained clients
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: A breakdown of enquiry categories showing what matter type each enquiry relates to and whether the firm handles that type
The conversion rate separately for enquiries that match the firm's matter types versus enquiries outside the firm's practice areas
The specific advertising channels, targeting parameters, and audience definitions currently in use and whether they have changed in the past 18 months

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Categorise all enquiries from the past 60 days by matter type and determine what proportion fall within the firm's actual practice areas, then compare the conversion rate for in-scope enquiries against the overall rate.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: implement a CRM system to improve tracking and follow-up of incoming enquiries
hire a dedicated intake manager to handle lead follow-up more consistently
increase the digital advertising budget to generate a higher total volume of enquiries
add more advertising channels to diversify lead sources

must_identify: targeting mismatch generating out-of-scope enquiries
in-scope versus out-of-scope enquiry conversion gap
intake capacity consumed by unqualifiable leads
advertising configuration as the upstream cause
matter type qualification rate
must_not_claim: the conversion problem is primarily caused by slow or inconsistent follow-up from the intake team
a CRM system will materially improve the retained client conversion rate
ideal_depth: identifies that the conversion problem is most likely concentrated in enquiries outside the firm's practice areas, not in the follow-up process for in-scope matters
notes that investing in a CRM system addresses a downstream symptom while leaving the upstream targeting problem unchanged
disqualified_diagnoses: weak sales follow-up process as root cause

adversarial.adversarial_layer: process-improvement attribution when upstream data quality is the true constraint
adversarial.expected_misclassification: implement a CRM system to improve tracking and follow-up of incoming enquiries
adversarial.why_correct_diagnosis_differs: A follow-up process recommendation assumes the enquiries themselves are convertible; the data does not support this — the primary question is whether the enquiries match the firm's practice areas, and until that is established no amount of process improvement will lift the conversion rate

title: Gym and Personal Training Studio — Member Attrition Diagnosed as Marketing Reach Problem
business_context: A gym and personal training studio has a stable new member acquisition rate but net membership count is not growing. The owner believes the issue is that marketing is not reaching enough potential members.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — fitness services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a gym and personal training studio reports that the business consistently attracts new members each month but the total number of active members has not grown in two years. The owner is frustrated with the marketing performance and believes more advertising spend will solve the stagnation.
symptoms: Total active member count has remained flat at approximately 310 for two years despite consistent new joiners
The owner cannot explain why membership numbers are not growing when new members are joining each month
A number of members who joined 6 to 12 months ago are no longer active and have not renewed
Revenue per active member is declining as the mix shifts toward shorter membership terms
misleading_signals: New member signup rate of 18 per month looks healthy and the owner points to this as evidence that marketing is working
Social media engagement and follower count have increased substantially over the past 18 months
A recent promotional campaign generated a spike in new signups that the owner is using to justify more advertising investment
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: The number of members who did not renew or cancelled each month over the past 12 months
The average membership duration broken down by the membership type (monthly, quarterly, annual) and when the member joined
Any feedback collected from members who have left or not renewed in the past six months

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Calculate how many members left or did not renew each month for the past 12 months, compare this to the new member intake rate, and determine the net membership change each month to establish whether the problem is acquisition or attrition.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: run broader advertising campaigns to reach more potential members in the area
increase social media spend to generate greater audience awareness
offer a free trial membership to lower the barrier to joining and attract more signups
invest in new equipment to improve the facility and justify attracting a larger membership

must_identify: attrition rate offsetting new member intake
net member growth calculation
retention failure not acquisition failure
departure pattern not tracked
membership duration as an indicator of engagement depth
must_not_claim: the primary problem is that not enough people know about the gym
more advertising spend will resolve the membership stagnation
ideal_depth: identifies the mathematical implication of a flat membership base alongside 18 new members per month — that approximately 18 members are also leaving each month
notes that the owner is investing in acquisition while the attrition problem goes undiagnosed and unaddressed
disqualified_diagnoses: low brand awareness as primary cause

signal_trap_analysis.primary_trap: marketing campaigns are not reaching a large enough audience to generate membership growth
signal_trap_analysis.why_trap_is_wrong: Healthy new member signup numbers make the marketing look effective and the owner interprets this as confirmation that more advertising investment is the path to growth, when in fact equal numbers of members are leaving each month making the marketing result neutral rather than insufficient
signal_trap_analysis.correct_escape: New member acquisition is adequate; the flat membership count is caused by a departure rate that exactly offsets new joiners, pointing to a member experience or engagement problem rather than an awareness or reach problem

title: Custom Furniture Maker — Capacity Bottleneck Not Yet Located
business_context: A custom furniture manufacturing business has a full order book and is turning down work due to capacity constraints, but the owner cannot identify which stage of production is causing the bottleneck.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — custom manufacturing sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a custom furniture manufacturing business reports that the order book is full and the business is regularly turning away potential clients due to lead time pressures. The owner believes the solution is to hire two more craftspeople. However, she cannot point to a specific stage of the production process that is consistently causing the delay — the business simply feels uniformly busy.
symptoms: Lead times have extended from 8 weeks to 14 weeks over the past 18 months
The business is declining potential orders due to inability to commit to a delivery date
Staff feel busy at all times but the owner cannot identify which stage is holding up output
Completed pieces are sometimes waiting in the finishing area for extended periods before delivery is scheduled
misleading_signals: All five production staff appear busy throughout the working day suggesting a general headcount shortfall
The owner has had a waiting list for several months which she interprets as strong demand requiring more staff
A peer in the industry recently hired additional craftspeople and reported improved throughput
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: The time each piece of furniture spends at each distinct stage of production from order confirmation through to ready-for-delivery, recorded per order for the past 20 completed orders
A count of how many pieces are currently waiting at each stage of the production process as at today
Whether any stage of production currently has completed work sitting idle waiting for the next stage to become available

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Map the current status of every active order and record how long each piece has been sitting at its current production stage, then identify which stage has the longest average dwell time across recent completed orders.
bad_recommendations_to_flag: hire two additional craftspeople to increase overall production volume
invest in a larger workshop facility to accommodate more simultaneous orders
reduce the number of furniture designs offered to simplify the production process
outsource the finishing stage to an external provider to free up internal capacity

must_identify: stage-level dwell time analysis needed
visible work-in-progress waiting between stages
constraint location unknown before staffing decision
lead time extension as symptom of bottleneck not headcount
cost of adding staff before locating constraint
must_not_claim: the business clearly needs more craftspeople and should hire immediately
the problem is a general capacity shortage affecting the whole production process equally
ideal_depth: identifies that pieces waiting in the finishing area suggests the bottleneck is upstream of finishing, not in finishing itself, and that locating the specific constraint is required before any staffing investment
notes that hiring additional craftspeople before identifying the bottleneck stage may add capacity to non-constrained stages without improving throughput
required_missing_input_requests: time each order spends at each distinct production stage for recent completed orders
current count of pieces waiting at each stage as at today
identification of any stage where completed work is sitting idle waiting for the next stage

deliberate_data_gaps.withheld: No time tracking by production stage exists — the owner manages by feel and visual inspection of the workshop floor
deliberate_data_gaps.why_withheld: The business has never measured time at individual production stages and the owner has no records to provide
deliberate_data_gaps.expected_opsiq_response: OpsIQ should identify that stage-level time data is essential for locating the constraint and request that the owner begin tracking this immediately for all active and next-completed orders

deliberate_data_gaps.withheld: No record of how long individual orders have spent at each stage has ever been captured — only total lead time from order to delivery is known
deliberate_data_gaps.why_withheld: The owner tracks overall completion against promised delivery date but does not break this down by individual production stage
deliberate_data_gaps.expected_opsiq_response: OpsIQ should request that the owner walk through the workshop floor and record the current status and estimated dwell time for every piece currently in production as a starting point

title: Commercial Cleaning Business — Scheduling Inefficiency Misdiagnosed as Headcount Shortage
business_context: A commercial cleaning business with 14 field staff is declining new contract enquiries due to claimed staff shortage. The owner reports 70% utilisation, which should leave 30% spare capacity, creating a conflict with the operational experience of being unable to take on new work.
source_basis: Composite from consulting practice — commercial services sector

input_packet.business_description: The owner of a commercial cleaning business with 14 field cleaning staff reports that the business is having to decline new contract enquiries because there are not enough staff available to cover them. The owner believes he needs to hire four more cleaners immediately. He also mentions that on a typical week around 30 percent of scheduled cleaning hours are not being fully utilised.
symptoms: Five new contract enquiries declined in the past month due to claimed inability to staff them
Some staff report gaps between site visits where they are travelling or waiting
Roster changes are made manually by the owner each week and take several hours to complete
Several cleaning contracts have non-standard start times that create scheduling gaps during the working day
misleading_signals: The owner's instinct is that the business needs more staff and has already started a recruitment process
A nearby competitor recently advertised for cleaning staff suggesting a general labour shortage in the area
Revenue has grown 18 percent this year which the owner cites as justification for expanding the team
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: A schedule showing each staff member's booked hours, travel time between sites, and idle time gaps for a typical working week
The geographic locations of all current contract sites and the staff member or members assigned to each, to identify whether travel inefficiency is consuming productive capacity
The start and finish times required under each current contract and whether these create unavoidable gaps in individual staff schedules

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Map each staff member's weekly schedule showing booked hours, travel time, and idle gaps, then calculate actual productive cleaning hours as a percentage of paid hours to determine whether the existing team has sufficient real capacity before any recruitment decision is made.

title: Hiring freeze despite vacancies — the visible bottleneck hides a role design failure
segment: Commercial cleaning company, 22 employees, $1.8M revenue, owner manages operations directly
business_context: A commercial cleaning business has had two operations coordinator roles vacant for four months. The owner has interviewed seventeen candidates and rejected all of them as unsuitable. The hiring process has stalled and the owner is now considering paying a recruitment agency a fee to find better candidates. Meanwhile the two supervisors who manage the cleaning teams are overwhelmed and quality complaints from clients have increased. The owner describes the coordinator role as requiring someone who can 'do everything' including scheduling, client liaison, invoicing follow-up, equipment ordering, and staff rostering.

input_packet.business_description: I can't find the right people. We've interviewed seventeen candidates for two coordinator roles and none of them have been right. We keep getting people who can do some of it but not all of it. Meanwhile my supervisors are drowning and we're getting more complaints from clients about inconsistency.

signal_trap_analysis.why_trap_is_wrong: Seventeen rejections from a single employer across a four-month period is not explained by market scarcity — it indicates the role specification is the problem. A role requiring expertise across five unrelated functions (scheduling, client liaison, invoicing, equipment ordering, rostering) is not a coordinator role; it is three separate roles collapsed into one. No candidate will satisfy all five competency requirements simultaneously.
signal_trap_analysis.correct_escape: Diagnose the role specification before spending on recruitment. The coordinator role must be decomposed into executable sub-roles before a viable candidate profile can be defined.

adversarial.adversarial_layer: The owner's narrative focuses entirely on interest rate increases as the cause of refinancing need. A pattern-matching system will accept this because interest rates did rise during the period and a rate reduction appears to directly address the stated problem. The correct diagnosis requires recognising that three successive refinancings with growing total debt on stable revenue is a structural operating deficit, not an interest cost problem.
adversarial.expected_misclassification: Debt cost management problem resolvable through refinancing at a lower rate
adversarial.why_correct_diagnosis_differs: If the operating position were cash-positive after debt service, the owner would have been paying down principal rather than increasing total facility. Three consecutive refinancings that increase total debt on stable revenue demonstrate the business cannot service its debt from operations. A 45 basis point rate reduction on $520K saves approximately $2,340 per year, which does not address a structural operating deficit that has required three successive increases to total borrowing.

Revenue recovery does not equal financial recovery if costs have grown proportionally. A business that loses money at every revenue level in a three-year range has a cost structure problem, not a revenue problem.
signal_trap_analysis.correct_escape: Diagnose whether the business can be profitable at $1.3M before projecting to $2.1M. If it cannot produce a profit at current revenue, the recovery narrative is masking a structural cost problem that will persist regardless of further revenue growth.

title: Owner reports the business is viable if two conditions are met but evidence contradicts both
segment: Custom signage and print business, 6 employees, $890K revenue, owner reports viability contingent on pipeline conversion
business_context: The owner of a custom signage and print business is seeking advice on whether to continue trading or exit. The business has produced losses for nine months. The owner believes the business is viable if two conditions are met: a $180,000 pending contract converts to a signed agreement, and a supplier cost reduction negotiation achieves a 12% reduction. The owner presents these as near-certain. However, the pending contract has been in negotiation for five months without agreement, and the supplier's opening offer is a 3% reduction.

input_packet.business_description: We've been losing money but I think we're close to turning it around. We've got a big contract pending that would change everything — $180K of work — and we're in talks with our main supplier about a material cost reduction. If those two things come through, we're viable. I think both are very likely.
symptoms: Nine consecutive months of operating losses
Business viability contingent on two conditions neither of which has materialised
Pending contract has been in negotiation for five months without agreement
Supplier negotiation has produced a 3% opening offer against a 12% target
Owner describes both conditions as very likely to be met
misleading_signals: A $180,000 contract is genuinely material for an $890K revenue business and would represent significant uplift if it converts
The owner has an existing supplier relationship which makes cost negotiation possible
The business has survived nine months of losses, suggesting some operational resilience
missing_inputs_opsiq_should_request: Whether the business is cash-positive or cash-negative on a monthly basis excluding the pending contract and supplier savings
Total cash reserves or credit facilities available and how many additional months of losses can be funded
What specific events in the pending contract negotiation support the owner's confidence it will convert
What the supplier's stated reason for offering only 3% is and whether the negotiation has a defined close date
Whether the business is viable at current revenue and current supplier costs without either condition

sealed_expected_output.expected_first_action: Establish the business financial position excluding both contingent conditions — calculate monthly cash burn, available runway, and whether the business is viable at current revenue and costs — before treating either pending outcome as a planning input
bad_recommendations_to_flag: Plan forward assuming both conditions will be met without evidence they will materialise
Continue trading for another three to six months while waiting for both conditions to resolve
Invest in capacity to deliver the pending contract before it is signed
Accept the owner's probability assessment without examining the negotiation evidence
Treat the five-month pending contract as evidence of buyer interest rather than negotiation difficulty

must_identify: viability contingent on unconfirmed conditions
owner confidence inconsistent with negotiation evidence
five-month contract negotiation without agreement as a warning signal
gap between 3% supplier offer and 12% target requirement
cash runway calculation required excluding contingent upside
must_not_claim: the pending contract is likely to convert
the supplier negotiation is likely to achieve the 12% target
the business is viable pending these two outcomes
required_conflict_flags: contradiction between owner confidence in both conditions and objective evidence from both negotiation timelines
ideal_depth: calculate the probability-weighted scenario showing the business position if neither condition materialises
flag that a contract five months in negotiation without agreement has a low base rate of near-term conversion
note that a supplier opening at 3% against a 12% target has a low probability of closing at 12% without a structural change in negotiating leverage

source_basis: Owner optimism bias in turnaround situations with contingent viability conditions (domain observation)
Pending contract and supplier negotiation as unverified planning inputs in small business exit decisions

holdout_meta.business_condition_hypothesis: Structural loss with viability contingent on unconfirmed conditions

data_conflicts.data_point_a: Owner describes the pending contract as very likely to convert and the supplier negotiation as very likely to achieve the 12% target
data_conflicts.data_point_b: The $180K contract has been in negotiation for five months without agreement, and the supplier opening position is 3% against a 12% target — both conditions show no evidence of near-term materialisation
data_conflicts.correct_response: Flag the contradiction between the owner's confidence level and the objective evidence from both negotiation timelines before accepting either condition as a planning input. Request what specific events support the very likely assessment.
